body:
Any way how we can reproduce that? Generally speaking, we're using OpenSSL in the backend, so it should usually work. The relevant code is  [netlib/tcp.py#L293-L321](https://github.com/mitmproxy/netlib/blob/b6af3fddf4ee2c45a722bd5087c86cee59b8cfa0/netlib/tcp.py#L293-L321).
Could it be possible that your server only supports SSLv3 or even v2? You need to pass `--ssl-version-server all/SSLv3` to enable that in mitmproxy.

Cheers,
Max

I was receiving this when attempting to watch requests for this URL: https://exchangedev.taskbox.co/Microsoft-Server-ActiveSync. 

Pretty sure it's not an SSL version issue, as I get the same error using the --ssl-version-server SSLv3 flag, but can connect just fine via 'openssl s_client -connect exchangedev.taskbox.co:443 -ssl3'.

That server is on the public internet, and you're welcome to try making some requests and see what happens.

Thanks for the quick response.
Not sure what's the issue here - once I remove the Host header from my request, it works. If I use openssl's s_client, it works everytime...

``` python
from netlib.tcp import TCPClient

c = TCPClient(("exchangedev.taskbox.co",443))
c.connect()
c.convert_to_ssl()
c.wfile.write("""GET /Microsoft-Server-ActiveSync HTTP/1.1
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.3; WOW64; rv:35.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/35.0
Accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,*/*;q=0.8
Accept-Language: de,en-US;q=0.7,en;q=0.3
Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate
Connection: keep-alive
Host: exchangedev.taskbox.co

""")
c.wfile.flush()
print c.rfile.readline()
```

My guess is that requesting a different path on with the same host would also work. That host+path combo is set up to (in Exchange parlance) "Accept" client certificates, instead of "Ignore" or "Require" (in which case I believe this would be expected behavior).

So, I'm pretty sure there's something different about the TLS context being used, I'm just not sure what. I would imagine that the server is requesting a client certificate somehow and then ignoring an empty response, but I'm not an TLS expert.

issue.title: Hello Request breaks pyOpenSSL

repository.name: pyopenssl
repository.description: A Python wrapper around the OpenSSL library

issue.body:
Hi there,

I tried to hunt down https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/issues/472 today and encountered a strange pyOpenSSL bug. If the server
1. requests renegotiation (`Hello Request`),
2. (unsuccessfully) asks for a client certificate during renegotation and then
3. sends some encrypted data, I cannot read that data using pyOpenSSL.

Here's my testcase - I think I'm doing nothing special:

``` python
from OpenSSL import SSL
import socket

ctx = SSL.Context(SSL.SSLv23_METHOD)
sock = SSL.Connection(ctx, socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM))
sock.connect(("exchangedev.taskbox.co", 443))
sock.do_handshake()

def dump_creds():
    crand = sock.client_random().encode("hex")
    masterkey = sock.master_key().encode("hex")
    with open("keys","ab") as f:
        f.write("CLIENT_RANDOM {} {}\r\n".format(crand, masterkey))

dump_creds()

sock.send("GET /Microsoft-Server-ActiveSync HTTP/1.1\r\n"
          "Host: exchangedev.taskbox.co\r\n"
          "\r\n"
          "\r\n")

try:
    print(sock.recv(1))
finally:
    dump_creds() # renegotiated master key
```

Here's the output:

```
C:\Users\user\git\mitmproxy\test\>python test.py
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "test.py", line 23, in <module>
    print(sock.recv(1))
  File "C:\Python27\lib\site-packages\OpenSSL\SSL.py", line 995, in recv
    self._raise_ssl_error(self._ssl, result)
  File "C:\Python27\lib\site-packages\OpenSSL\SSL.py", line 847, in _raise_ssl_error
    raise WantReadError()
OpenSSL.SSL.WantReadError
```

Now, that clearly looks like I'm not getting any data back. However, looking at Wireshark, I see this:

![Wireshark Output](https://maximilianhils.com/upload/2015-02/2015-02-12_03-00-31.png)

Similarly, using `openssl s_client -connect exchangedev.taskbox.co:443`, I get the response.

Here's the [pcap dump](https://maximilianhils.com/upload/2015-02/dump.pcapng) with the corresponding [SSL keys](https://maximilianhils.com/upload/2015-02/keys) for Wireshark (Protocol Options -> SSL -> Master-Secret log file). For the lazy, here's also a screenshot:

![Wireshark screenshot](https://maximilianhils.com/upload/2015-02/2015-02-12_03-04-15.png)

The server mentioned above is on the public internet, and according to https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/issues/472#issuecomment-73786789 you're welcome to use it for testing. If there's anything else I can help with, please let me know! :smiley:

Thanks!
Max

body:
This seems to be an issue with pyOpenSSL - I opened up a ticket there: https://github.com/pyca/pyopenssl/issues/190

Cheers,
Max

issue.title: Add Option to Log SSL Session Keys for Wireshark Compatibility

repository.name: mitmproxy
repository.description: An interactive TLS-capable intercepting HTTP proxy for penetration testers and software developers.

issue.body:
Currently, we can inspect SSL traffic to the proxy by instructing it to use ciphers without perfect forward secrecy only. As far as I know, inspecting the upstream connection is hard possibly without manual intervention. To debug issues like https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/issues/472, it would be nice to have a command line option to dump the SSL keys for Wireshark.

There are two complications:
1. We should log keys if renegotation during the session occurs (see https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/issues/472), not just after the handshake. I hope we can use the pyOpenSSL equivalent of [SSL_CTX_set_info_callback](https://www.openssl.org/docs/ssl/SSL_CTX_set_info_callback.html) for this?
2. Writing to a file from different connection threads requires synchronization.

The following works for single-threaded code:

``` python
def dump_creds(sock):
    crand = sock.client_random().encode("hex")
    masterkey = sock.master_key().encode("hex")
    with open("keys","ab") as f:
        f.write("CLIENT_RANDOM {} {}\r\n".format(crand, masterkey))
```

body: I am experiencing this problem too... Is there any workaround?
@GordonMcKinney, this is not a mitmproxy bug and I don't see a way how we could work around this issue. :confused: For now, you can only ask the pyOpenSSL guys to look at it.

OSX Safari shows the same fault. So we're looking at IIS plus strict and non-strict compliance from client libraries.
